patch.value: Resolve validate duplicate issue-code GH-209 warning without changelog drag

pm validate metadata warns validate_metadata_duplicate_issue_codes for GH-209 shared by closed items pm-1byt (exit-13 top-level-await fix) and pm-25se (OTLP export follow-up). Both live in shipped release buckets; renaming either title now would move it into [Unreleased] because pm-changelog buckets by updated_at (known trap). Resolve by either (a) teaching issue-code dedupe to exempt explicit 'follow-up' titled items so distinct logical work sharing a GH code is not flagged, or (b) performing the rename in a dedicated tracker-only migration where the changelog is regenerated and reviewed in the same commit.

pm validate reports duplicate_issue_codes_count: 0 (or the GH-209 pair is exempted by an agreed follow-up rule with a spec); changelog:pm:check stays green in the same change; no closed item silently migrates release buckets.

## Context
`pm validate` metadata check warns `validate_metadata_duplicate_issue_codes: 1` — issue code GH-209 is shared by two CLOSED items:
- pm-1byt "GH-209: successful pm mutations can exit 13 from unsettled top-level await" (closed 2026-06-12)
- pm-25se "GH-209 follow-up: OTEL span export keeps the CLI alive ~10s (and can exit 13) when the traces endpoint is unreachable" (closed 2026-06-14)

Issue-code extraction is title-prefix based, so the "GH-209 follow-up:" prefix collides with the original. Both items are legitimate distinct work; this is arguably a validator false-positive rather than a data error.

## Why this can't be fixed by a simple rename
pm-changelog buckets closed items by `updated_at`. Touching either closed item now would drag it out of its shipped release section (2026.6.x) into `[Unreleased]`, corrupting the historical changelog and failing `changelog:pm:check` review expectations. This is the known changelog-bucket trap that has bitten twice before.

## Options (pick one)
1. **Validator exemption (preferred):** teach the issue-code dedupe to treat an explicit "follow-up" marker (e.g. title starting `GH-NNN follow-up:`) as a distinct logical code, with a spec pinning the exemption. Fixes the class, touches no closed items, zero changelog risk.
2. **Tracker-only rename migration:** rename pm-25se's title prefix (e.g. `GH-209-FU:`) in a dedicated tracker-only commit where the changelog is regenerated and the bucket move is reviewed/accepted explicitly as part of the same change.

## Evidence
- `pm validate` remediation_hint: "Items pm-1byt, pm-25se share issue code \"GH-209\"; rename or merge so each logical code maps to one item."
- Remediation-registry entry for this warning class already exists (closed pm-sdbo).

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Unblocked 2026-07-26. The constraint that held this item was that a metadata write on a long-closed item re-buckets it into the current changelog section, because attribution resolved through closed_at ?? updated_at ?? created_at and 1,488 of 1,795 terminal items carried no closed_at. That is no longer true.

Every terminal item now carries a release identifier derived from the tag whose window contains its close event, taken from its immutable history stream: 1,782 stamped, 13 deliberately left unstamped because they close after the newest tag and therefore belong to the pending window. The derivation was validated against ground truth before any write — for the 307 items that already had closed_at, the history-derived instant matched on 307 and disagreed on 0.

The generator honours the release field as the attribution authority under --all-release-tags, which was proved directly rather than assumed: stamping a closed item, which moved its updated_at to now, produced a byte-identical CHANGELOG.md. After the full backfill, regeneration moved 295 items and every one of those moves matched the derivation, with no items added or removed and the Unreleased section unchanged.

The practical consequence for this item: the backfill work it describes can now proceed as ordinary mutations without changelog churn, and the ordering constraint that deferred it no longer applies. Evidence and method are recorded on pm-3j6it6.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Measured 2026-07-29: the evidence that would suppress this false positive is already stored, in a typed edge the detector never reads.

The pair is unchanged. pm-1byt titled "GH-209: successful pm mutations can exit 13 from unsettled top-level await", release v2026.6.13, parent pm-mpbb. pm-25se titled "GH-209 follow-up: OTEL span export keeps the CLI alive ~10s (and can exit 13) when the traces endpoint is unreachable", release v2026.6.16, parent pm-5oj5. Distinct work, distinct release buckets, distinct capability epics.

The new fact. pm-25se already carries a dependency row of kind discovered_from pointing at pm-1byt, alongside a related row to the same id. The tracker therefore already asserts, in its own typed relationship vocabulary, exactly the proposition the check is missing: this item is derived from that item, so the shared code is inheritance rather than collision. No new data has to be authored for option (a) to become decidable.

Why the check cannot see it. findDuplicateIssueCodes in src/core/governance/issue-codes.ts accepts an IssueCodeItem of four fields: id, title, parent, duplicate_of. It already models two by-design exemptions and both are honest ones. Closed-as-duplicate is read from duplicate_of, added for GH-278. Parent-prefix sharing is read from the scalar parent, added for GH-275, and its own docstring explains that resolving the reference against the whole corpus rather than the same-code group would suppress genuinely colliding siblings. The exemption logic is well reasoned; the input shape is the limit. The function is handed no dependency rows at all, so a derivation edge cannot influence it even in principle.

That makes this a channel-coverage gap, not a heuristic-tuning problem. The tracker records "these two items are the same lineage" through at least three channels: the scalar parent, duplicate_of, and the typed derivation kinds discovered_from, supersedes and incident_from. Governance reads exactly the first two. The GH-275 exemption is the proof that the maintainers already intended by-design reuse to be exempt; the GH-209 pair is the same intent expressed through the derivation channel instead of the hierarchy channel, and it is flagged only because of which channel it used. This is the same shape as the hierarchy divergence on pm-vk7zek, where one relation has two encodings and a governance surface consults one of them.

Consequence for the two options in the description. Option (b), the rename migration, is now the worse choice: it would delete true information from a title in order to satisfy a check that already has access to the truth by another route. Option (a) should be narrowed. The rule should not key on the literal word "follow-up" in a title, which is unenforceable prose that any author can omit or misspell. It should key on the derivation edge: within a code group, drop any item that carries a derivation-kind dependency row pointing at another item in the same group, mirroring the existing parent rule exactly, including its deliberate same-group-only resolution. The word "follow-up" in the title then becomes a courtesy to human readers rather than a load-bearing token.

Test shape this implies. A negative control is required and is cheap: two items sharing a code with no edge of any kind between them must still be reported, and the same pair with a related row between them must also still be reported, because related is not a derivation kind and asserting similarity is not asserting lineage. The positive control is the live pair, which needs no fixture authoring.

Recorded during 2026-07-29 governance repair. No mutation was made to either GH-209 item; the warning is deliberately left standing so the fix has a live subject.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Disposition of the last remaining duplicate 2026-07-30 (evening). The warning is down to one code and that one code is a false positive against the data, not a defect in it.

GH-209 maps to two items: one for successful mutations exiting 13 from an unsettled top-level await, and one follow-up for an OTEL span export keeping the CLI alive for around ten seconds and reaching the same exit code when the traces endpoint is unreachable. Both are closed, one stamped to the 2026-06-13 release and the other to 2026-06-16, so they were delivered a release apart. They are two distinct defects that a single upstream report surfaced, and the second was found while fixing the first. The remediation hint says to rename or merge, and both of those would be wrong: merging discards the fact that two separate fixes shipped in two separate releases, and renaming edits a historical title so that a check stops complaining.

So the residual work on this chore is on the check rather than on the corpus. One issue legitimately produces more than one item when the report surfaces more than one defect, and the check currently cannot express that. The two candidate shapes are an explicit follow-up or derived-from relation between the two items, which already exists as a typed edge kind and could satisfy the check by structure rather than by naming, or an allowance in the check for one primary plus N derived items per code. The first is better because it makes the relationship queryable rather than merely tolerated.

Recording the numbers so a later pass can tell resolution from suppression: duplicate_issue_codes_count is 1, ids pm-1byt and pm-25se, and no other code in the corpus has more than one item. If a future run shows zero without either of those two items gaining a typed relation or the check gaining an allowance, someone renamed history and the class is not actually closed.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Second instance observed 2026-08-03, and it changes what the class means.

duplicate_issue_codes is now count 2. The prior sole member is GH-209 on pm-1byt and pm-25se. The new member is GH-779 on pm-ajaskl, closed 2026-07-28, and pm-wnbk2l, closed 2026-08-02, whose title states recurrence explicitly and which carries a discovered_from edge to its predecessor.

Both pairs share one shape: two correctly filed, correctly closed items describing two real occurrences of one identity, where the second occurrence had nowhere to record that identity except the title. The check-side disposition already recorded here is therefore confirmed and strengthened. The remediation hint that proposes renaming or merging is wrong for both pairs, because in both cases the shared code is the only durable statement that the occurrences belong together.

The wider consequence is that this check is currently the project's only recurrence detector, and it reports its findings as defects. That gap now has its own owner covering the missing relation in the dependency-kind lexicon, cited from here. When the relation exists, the correct disposition for this class becomes mechanical rather than judgemental: a shared code between items joined by an explicit recurrence edge is expected and reported as such, and a shared code without one stays a warning.
